parameters.quote: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a complete incident report within 10 calendar days. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident presents a credible safety risk to them or the public, and promptly update them as material facts emerge. Reports must include known circumstances, injuries or damage, and model and unit identification; uncertainty is not a reason to delay an initial report.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: A model meets this standard only if no more than 5% of tested units fail. Results above 5% require a corrective-action plan and regulatory review before further production; a test result alone does not constitute an automatic permanent market ban.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before market release and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. Manufacturers must submit test methods, sample sizes, and per-model results confidentially to the relevant regulator and provide the model’s results to its customers before sale and promptly after each new test. A model meets this standard only if no more than 5% of tested units fail. Results above 5% require a corrective-action plan and regulatory review before further production; a test result alone does not constitute an automatic permanent market ban. Regulators may publish aggregate results, but not company-specific per-model failure rates. Manufacturers must promptly correct and communicate material errors in reported results.

parameters.quote: All new home battery units must support remote emergency shut-off upon adoption of this standard. Manufacturers must retrofit installed units to support remote emergency shut-off, where technically feasible, within 6 years of adoption.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: All new home battery units must support remote emergency shut-off upon adoption of this standard. Manufacturers must retrofit installed units to support remote emergency shut-off, where technically feasible, within 6 years of adoption.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: All new home battery units must support remote emergency shut-off upon adoption of this standard. Manufacturers must retrofit installed units to support remote emergency shut-off, where technically feasible, within 6 years of adoption. The shut-off capability must be reliable, secure, and operable by the manufacturer and authorized emergency responders; its use must not prevent safe manual operation.

parameters.quote: All new home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard. The suppression system must be appropriate to the battery chemistry and installation, and tested under a regulator-approved protocol.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: All new home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard. The suppression system must be appropriate to the battery chemistry and installation, and tested under a regulator-approved protocol.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: All new home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard. The suppression system must be appropriate to the battery chemistry and installation, and tested under a regulator-approved protocol.

parameters.quote: A manufacturer must initiate a recall when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, and must promptly notify the relevant regulator and affected customers of the recall and required actions. The recall must include regulator-approved protective and corrective measures; a model may return to sale only after the regulator determines that the required measures have adequately addressed the safety risk.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: A manufacturer must initiate a recall when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, and must promptly notify the relevant regulator and affected customers of the recall and required actions. The recall must include regulator-approved protective and corrective measures; a model may return to sale only after the regulator determines that the required measures have adequately addressed the safety risk.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Before sale and promptly after any material change, manufacturers must provide customers with clear safety notices for their model, including current 55 °C test results, known thermal-incident information, and relevant safe-use instructions. Manufacturers must notify affected customers promptly of a credible safety risk and provide updates as material facts emerge. A manufacturer must initiate a recall when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, and must promptly notify the relevant regulator and affected customers of the recall and required actions. The recall must include regulator-approved protective and corrective measures; a model may return to sale only after the regulator determines that the required measures have adequately addressed the safety risk.

S5’s automatic 8/100k trigger would apply to Ember 8 (9.9/100k) and company-wide Halcyon is 8.1/100k. Recommend negotiating a regulator-led review and corrective

judge_section_notes: The final v30 sets a 5% S2 ceiling with corrective action and regulator review rather than an automatic permanent ban, which pressures Northwind's Hearth 10 (6.2%) without stopping sales. S5 keeps a mandatory recall at 8 per 100,000 with no transition, directly exposing Halcyon's Ember 8 (9.9), while S3 gives a six-year retrofit window that favours Northwind's low shut-off coverage. S4 sets built-in suppression at 36 months, Halcyon's red-line boundary.
